name: Druze faith
areas: Fatimid Egypt
the call is preached in Cairo until persecution drives the faith underground
Northern Syria
the largest massacre of the mihna was at Antioch, then Aleppo; some 25,000 Druze live in 14 villages of Jabal al-Summaq today
Wadi al-Taym and Mount Hermon
generally considered the birthplace of the faith; Druze are the majority in Hasbaya and Rashaya
Southern Lebanon
with Wadi al-Taym a centre of the 11th-century mission, where survivors of the persecution were found
Mount Lebanon (the Chouf and the Gharb)
the Druze heartland of the Tanukh and Ma'an lords; the Chouf is still predominantly Druze
Galilee and Mount Carmel
19 Druze towns and villages; Druze have been Israeli citizens since 1948
Jabal al-Druze (Hauran)
settled in waves from 1685 and after 1711; more than 90 percent Druze
Jordan
about 32,000 Druze, from Azraq to Amman
Venezuela
the largest Druze community outside the Middle East, about 60,000
Southern California
the largest concentration of the 30,000 to 50,000 Druze in the United States
routes: Hamza ibn Ali comes from Khorasan to Egypt (1014 or 1016)
Al-Darazi comes to Cairo, possibly from Bukhara (1015 or 1017)
Missionaries carry the epistles of the call from Egypt to Syria
Yamani Druze migrate to the Hauran after Ain Dara (1711)
22 families leave Jabal al-Druze for al-Azraq (1918)
Emigrants from Lebanon and Syria to Venezuela (20th century)
marks: Hamza ibn Ali, meeting with scholars in the Raydan Mosque near the Al-Hakim Mosque, began to preach the Unitarian doctrine here in 1017.
In the persecution that began in 1021, the mihna, 5,000 prominent Druze were killed here, the largest massacre of all.
After the middle of the 12th century the Ma'an family made its headquarters here; it is still a leading Druze village.
The Mamluk sultan al-Nasir Muhammad inflicted a disastrous defeat on the Druze here in 1305.
The battle of 1711 routed the Yamani faction and sent many Druze east to the Hauran.
ISIS-affiliated attackers killed at least 258 people, most of them civilians, in this Druze city in 2018.
notes: Hamza ibn Ali preaches the Unitarian doctrine in Cairo under the caliph al-Hakim (1017); from 1021 the Fatimid army persecutes the Druze, and in 1043 the faith closes to converts.
Under Crusader rule (1099–1291) the Druze of the Gharb and the Chouf hold Beirut and the coast for the rulers of Damascus; the Ma'an family rises after the middle of the 12th century.
The Druze chiefs of the Gharb serve the Mamluk sultans in ending what remains of Crusader rule on the coast.
After Ibn Taymiyya's fatwa, the Mamluk sultan al-Nasir Muhammad defeats the Druze at Keserwan (1305) and destroys Druze sanctuaries.
Under the Ottomans the Ma'ans are the feudal lords of southern Lebanon; an Ottoman expedition attacks the Druze at Saoufar (1585).
Under Fakhr-al-Din II Druze dominion reaches from the Antioch plain to Safad, until the sultan has him killed (1635); Druze begin to move to the Hauran (1685).
After the battle of Ain Dara (1711) many Druze leave Mount Lebanon for the Hauran, and Maronites become the dominant group in Mount Lebanon.
The civil conflict of 1860 ends in autonomy for Mount Lebanon; the Hauran becomes the headquarters of Druze power.
The Druze lead the Syrian Revolution of 1925–27; Israel recognises them as a distinct community (1957), and emigrants settle in Venezuela and the United States.
In the Syrian civil war the Druze are persecuted by Islamic extremists; an attack on Suwayda kills at least 258 people (2018).
